July 1 (UPI) -- United Nations High Commission for Refugees and other international organizations warned that Venezuela's humanitarian crisis is deteriorating rapidly following the twin earthquakes that struck the country on June 24.

The collapse of basic services, severe food shortages and the loss of critical infrastructure have deepened an emergency affecting a population that was already facing widespread humanitarian needs.

Initial assessments conducted by the UNHCR between June 26 and June 27 in La Guaira, the Capital District, Miranda, Aragua and Carabobo states confirmed a rapid deterioration in living conditions across the affected areas.

The agency warned of growing protection risks for nearly 16,000 displaced families who lack safe shelter, clean drinking water and electricity. It estimated that 39% of those families are living on the streets, in public squares or in makeshift shelters without basic sanitation.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_71830" });

For that reason, the World Food Programme on Tuesday launched an emergency appeal for $50 million to provide three months of assistance to about 500,000 people in Venezuela.

The WFP said it has already distributed emergency food rations to 1,200 people and currently has 3,000 metric tons of food stored in the country, enough to feed more than 10,000 families for two months.

"The need for food, safe drinking water, shelter and basic services is immediate and critical," the agency's representative in Venezuela, Stephanie Hochstetter, said on Tuesday during the daily press briefing by the U.N. secretary-general's spokesperson.

Hochstetter warned that the earthquakes did not strike a country under normal circumstances, but one where food insecurity was already a structural problem.

According to a preliminary NASA assessment, nearly 59,000 buildings may have collapsed, particularly along Venezuela's central Caribbean coast, La Guaira state and the Caracas metropolitan corridor.

Venezuelan authorities reported in their latest official update that 1,943 people were killed and about 10,000 were injured. However, U.N. Resident Coordinator Gianluca Rampolla said the collapse of numerous buildings suggests the final death toll could be significantly higher.

The United Nations has coordinated with the Venezuelan government to procure 10,000 body bags. The organization also estimates that as many as 50,000 people remain missing.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_96816" });

Acting President Delcy Rodriguez said 38 hospitals were damaged by the twin earthquakes, increasing pressure on a healthcare system that was already struggling before the disaster.

The World Health Organization warned of an imminent risk of disease outbreaks, including dengue fever, measles and diphtheria, driven by overcrowding and contamination of water systems after sewage infrastructure collapsed.

Pedro Fernandez, coordinator of Doctors United for Venezuela, told DW that the regions hardest hit by the earthquakes were already experiencing severe humanitarian conditions before the disaster.

He said affected families were already facing food shortages and hospitals lacked essential supplies before the earthquakes, "so the international response has been critical to helping the injured."

"Unfortunately, we are seeing strict controls over the receipt of aid and the distribution of food," Fernandez said.

He said people across Venezuela have mobilized to send assistance to the hardest-hit areas, but government controls have prevented much of that aid from reaching those in need.

"This has slowed the delivery of both domestic and international assistance. In many areas, aid is arriving too late and warning signs of epidemiological outbreaks are already emerging," he said.

The situation facing children remains one of the greatest concerns.

The United Nations Children's Fund and Save the Children reported that nearly 680,000 children require urgent assistance. In Caracas alone, 432 schools suffered severe damage, significantly disrupting access to education.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_23906" });

UNICEF also warned that children have become separated from their parents amid the chaos following the earthquakes. In response, the U.N. Protection Cluster launched a campaign to identify unaccompanied children, locate their relatives and accelerate family reunification.

Before the earthquakes, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs had estimated that about 7.9 million Venezuelans already required priority humanitarian assistance because of soaring inflation, insufficient household income and limited access to essential public services.
